who: Tobit was an Israelite of the tribe of Naphtali, carried off as a captive to Nineveh. There he fed the hungry and buried the dead, even when the king hunted him for it. Then he went blind. His son Tobias set out on a journey with a stranger, who turned out to be the angel Raphael.

facts.label: Tribe
facts.text: **Naphtali**, one of the northern tribes of Israel. He came from **Thisbe**, in Galilee.

facts.label: Lived
facts.text: In exile in **Nineveh**, the capital of Assyria. His book sets him under three kings: **Enemessar**, **Sennacherib** and **Sarchedonus**, the Esarhaddon of history.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: His wife **Anna**, of his own family, and one son, **Tobias**. He lived to see six grandsons. His nephew **Achiacharus** served the king.

facts.label: Work
facts.text: The king's **buyer**, until the roads to Media became unsafe under Sennacherib.

facts.label: Known for
facts.text: **Giving alms** and **burying the dead** of his people, even when the king wanted him killed for it.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Tobias**, the same name as his son, in Jerome's Latin and the Douay Bible. Older books call him **Tobias the elder**. Both names come from the Hebrew word for **good**.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: In **Nineveh**, in his bed, very old. The Greek text used on this page says he was **158**. Jerome's Latin says **102**. Anna was buried beside him.

facts.label: His book
facts.text: The **Book of Tobit**, 14 short chapters. It is in **Catholic** and **Orthodox** Bibles, but not in the **Hebrew Bible**. Protestant Bibles that print it put it among the **Apocrypha**.

facts.label: Written
facts.text: By an unknown writer, at a date still argued over. The *Jewish Encyclopedia* of 1906 thought **between 200 and 50 BC** most likely.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: Blind, with **Anna** and the **kid goat**, or having his eyes healed with the **fish's gall**. Rembrandt painted his story again and again.

moments.title: Alone to Jerusalem
moments.text: Tobit grew up in Galilee, in the tribe of Naphtali. His father died and left him an orphan. When his whole tribe turned away from the temple in Jerusalem, he did not. “I alone went often to Jerusalem at the feasts.” He brought his first fruits to the priests, and gave a tenth of his harvest to the Levites. He spent a second tenth in Jerusalem every year, and gave away a third, as his grandmother Deborah had taught him.

moments.title: Bread for the hungry
moments.text: Tobit married Anna, of his own family, and they had a son, Tobias. Then the Assyrians carried him off to Nineveh. His relatives there ate the food of the Gentiles, but he kept himself from it, “because I remembered God with all my soul.” He rose to be the king's buyer, and on a journey to Media he left ten talents of silver in trust with a man named Gabael. At home he cared for his own people. “I gave my bread to the hungry, and my garments to the naked.” If he saw one of them dead and thrown out on the wall of Nineveh, he buried him.

moments.title: Hunted by the king
moments.text: King Sennacherib came back fleeing from Judea, and in his rage he killed many of the exiles. Tobit buried them in secret, and when the king looked for the bodies, they could not be found. Then a man of Nineveh told the king who had buried them. Tobit hid, and fled for his life. Everything he owned was taken, “save my wife Anna and my son Tobias.” Within fifty-five days, two of the king's own sons killed him. The new king put Tobit's nephew Achiacharus over all his accounts, and Achiacharus asked for Tobit. He came home to Nineveh.

moments.title: The dinner he left
moments.text: At Pentecost a good dinner was set before him. Seeing so much food, he sent Tobias out to bring home a poor man of their people to share it. “Behold, I wait for you.” Tobias came back with news. One of their people had been strangled and thrown out in the marketplace. “Before I had tasted anything, I sprang up.” Tobit carried the body into a room, and ate his bread in sorrow. After sunset he dug a grave and buried the man. His neighbours laughed at him. “He is no longer afraid to be put to death for this matter; and yet he fled away. Behold, he buries the dead again.”

moments.title: The sparrows
moments.text: Unclean from the burial, Tobit slept that night by the wall of his courtyard, with his face uncovered. He did not know there were sparrows in the wall. Their warm droppings fell into his open eyes, and “white films came over my eyes.” The doctors could not help him. His nephew Achiacharus looked after him for a time.

moments.title: The kid
moments.text: Now Anna kept them, weaving cloth for others. One day her employers paid her wages and gave her a young goat as well. Tobit heard it bleat. “Where did this kid come from? Is it stolen? Give it back to the owners.” She told him it was a gift. He did not believe her, and he was ashamed of her. She answered him back: “Where are your alms and your righteous deeds? Behold, you and all your works are known.”

moments.title: Two prayers
moments.text: Grieved, Tobit wept and prayed to die. “Command my spirit to be taken from me, that I may be released, and become earth.” That same day, far away in Ecbatana in Media, a young woman named Sarah prayed too. She had been given to seven husbands, and a demon, Asmodaeus, had killed each one before the marriage began. Her father's maids mocked her for it. Both prayers were heard “before the glory of the great God.” God sent the angel Raphael to heal them both.

moments.title: A guide for the road
moments.text: Sure he would die soon, Tobit remembered the silver he had left in Media. He gave Tobias a father's advice, and sent him to fetch it. Tobias found a man who knew the way, and brought him in. Tobit wanted to know his family first. The stranger said he was Azarias, a kinsman, and Tobit offered him a drachma a day. He did not know he was hiring an angel. Anna wept to see her son go. “Don't worry, my sister,” Tobit told her. “For a good angel will go with him.” So they set off, and the young man's dog went with them.

moments.title: The fish and the bride
moments.text: At the river Tigris a fish leaped out of the water at Tobias. The angel told him to catch it, and to keep its heart, liver and gall. At Ecbatana they stayed with Raguel, Tobit's kinsman, whose only daughter was Sarah. Raguel kissed Tobias and wept. “You are the son of an honest and good man.” He gave Tobias his daughter, though seven men had died before him. On the wedding night Tobias burned the heart and liver, and the demon fled “into the uppermost parts of Egypt, and the angel bound him.” Tobias and Sarah rose and prayed. That night Raguel dug a grave, “Lest he also should die.” A maid found them both asleep, and he had the grave filled in.

moments.title: Counting the days
moments.text: Raguel kept Tobias for the fourteen days of the wedding feast. At home, Tobit counted every day. Had his son been held up? Was Gabael dead? Anna was sure her son had died. She went out every day to watch the road he had taken, and ate nothing all day long. “Hold your peace,” Tobit told her. “Don't worry. He is in good health.”

moments.title: His eyes opened
moments.text: Anna, watching the road, saw them coming, and ran to throw her arms around her son. Tobit went toward the door and stumbled, and his son ran and caught hold of him. As the angel had told him, Tobias rubbed the fish's gall on his father's eyes. “Cheer up, my father.” The white films peeled away from the corners of his eyes, and he saw his son. He fell on his neck and wept. “Blessed are You, O God, and blessed is Your name forever! Blessed are all Your holy angels! For You scourged, and had mercy on me. Behold, I see my son Tobias.” He went out to the gate of Nineveh to meet his new daughter-in-law, and all who saw him marvelled.

moments.title: “I am Raphael”
moments.text: Tobit told his son to pay the guide well, and they offered him half of all they had brought home. Then he took them both aside. He told them to bless God and give thanks, and to give alms. God had sent him, he said, to heal Tobit and Sarah. “I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels which present the prayers of the saints and go in before the glory of the Holy One.” Father and son fell on their faces in fear. “Don't be afraid,” he said. “Write in a book all the things which have been done.” Then he rose, and they saw him no more.

words.note: Tobit's words are all in his own book. Every line from it on this page is from the World English Bible. Other Bible lines are from the Berean Standard Bible.

feature.q: For He scourges, and shows mercy. He leads down to the grave, and brings up again.
feature.ctx: After his eyes were opened and the angel had gone, Tobit wrote a prayer of rejoicing.

quotes.q: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don't let your eye be envious. Don't turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won't be turned away from you.
quotes.who: To his son, before the journey.

quotes.q: If you have little, don't be afraid to give alms according to that little.
And what you yourself hate, do to no man.
quotes.who: The Golden Rule, the other way round. Jesus gave it as “do to others as you would have them do to you.”

quotes.q: Don't let the wages of any man who works for you wait with you, but give it to him out of hand.
quotes.who: On paying a worker the same day.

quotes.q: In idleness is decay and great lack; for idleness is the mother of famine.
Ask counsel of every man who is wise, and don't despise any counsel that is profitable.

myths.claim: Tobit is the one who travels with the angel and catches the fish.
myths.truth: It is his son, **Tobias**. Tobit stayed at home in Nineveh, blind, while the boy made the journey with Raphael and the dog, and caught the fish. Orthodox icons of the archangel show the same scene: Raphael leading Tobias, who carries the fish.

cite.text: Tobit 5:16 to 6:5; OCA, Synaxis of the Archangel Michael and the Other Bodiless Powers

myths.claim: Tobit and Tobias are two spellings of one man.
myths.truth: They are father and son. The Greek copies call the father Tobit and the son Tobias. But Jerome's Latin, and the Douay Bible made from it, call them both Tobias. That is why older books speak of the elder and the younger Tobias.

myths.claim: God struck him blind for his sins.
myths.truth: His book says sparrows' droppings fell into his eyes, the night after a burial. Anna's taunt and his own prayer both wonder about sin, and Augustine heard people say of any blind man, “God is angry with him”. Jerome's Latin gives a different reason. God allowed the trial so that “an example might be given to posterity of his patience, as also of holy Job.” The angel tells him, “because thou wast acceptable to God, it was necessary that temptation should prove thee.”

cite.text: Tobit 2:9-14 and 3:3; Augustine, Sermon 38 on the New Testament; Tobias 2:12 and 12:13, in the Douay Bible

myths.claim: Raphael is in every Bible, like Michael and Gabriel.
myths.truth: He is named only in the *Book of Tobit*, so a Bible without it never names him. There he calls himself “one of the seven holy angels”, and Revelation too speaks of “the seven angels who stand before God”. Of those seven, says the *Catholic Encyclopedia*, only Michael, Gabriel and Raphael are named in Scripture. The other names come from the *Book of Enoch* and later writings.

extras.title: His book
extras.lede: The *Book of Tobit* is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, but not in the Hebrew Bible or most Protestant ones. Whether its story is history is argued over too. Here each side speaks for itself.

items.title: Catholic: part of the Bible
items.text: The Catholic Church counts Tobit among the books of the Old Testament. It calls such books deuterocanonical: books of the Greek Old Testament that are not in the Hebrew Bible. The councils of Hippo, in 393, and Carthage, in 397, listed Tobit, and the Council of Trent settled it for Catholics in 1546.
items.quote: Despite the rejection of Tobias from the Protestant Canon, its place in the Christian Canon of Holy Writ is undoubted.

items.title: Orthodox: read in the Church
items.text: The Orthodox Old Testament follows the Greek, so Tobit is in it. Orthodox voices describe it in two ways. The *Longer Catechism* of Philaret of Moscow cites Athanasius: such books were appointed “to be read by proselytes who are preparing for admission into the Church.” The Synod of Jerusalem in 1672 went further, and named Tobit as Scripture:
items.quote: For we judge these also to be with the other genuine Books of Divine Scripture genuine parts of Scripture.

cite.text: The Confession of Dositheus, question 3, tr. J. N. W. B. Robertson (1899); the Longer Catechism, question 36, tr. R. W. Blackmore

items.title: Protestant: useful, not binding
items.text: Luther printed Tobit among the Apocrypha, and called it useful and good for Christians to read. The Church of England reads such books “for example of life and instruction of manners”, but not to establish any doctrine. The *Westminster Confession* of 1647 is sharper:
items.quote: The books commonly called Apocrypha, not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the Canon of the Scripture; and therefore are of no authority in the Church of God, nor to be any otherwise approved, or made use of, than other human writings.

cite.text: The Westminster Confession, chapter 1; the Thirty-Nine Articles, Article 6, in Philip Schaff's The Creeds of Christendom

items.title: Jewish: never in the Hebrew Bible
items.text: The rabbis never counted Tobit among their holy books, though Jews copied it in Aramaic and Hebrew: pieces of five copies were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. The *Jewish Encyclopedia* of 1906 describes it:
items.quote: A late Jewish work, never received into the Jewish canon

items.title: Read as history
items.text: The Fathers told Tobit's story as fact. In 1912 the *Catholic Encyclopedia* still defended it. The trouble with some names and dates, it said, comes from a text that has reached us in poor shape, and the arguments against its history are “mere conjectures”.
items.quote: Until recently there never was question among Catholics in regard to the historicity of Tobias.

items.title: Read as a story that teaches
items.text: Many scholars read it as a story told to teach, not as a record. Its opening is already a puzzle: 2 Kings says Tiglath-pileser carried Naphtali away, not the king Tobit names. The *Jewish Encyclopedia* praised it as one of “the most delightful of short stories”. Luther had left the question open. Our translation:
items.quote: If it is history, it is a fine and holy history. If it is a poem, it is truly a good, beautiful, wholesome and useful poem and play, by a gifted poet.

cite.text: Luther, preface to Tobit, 1534; 2 Kings 15:29; Catholic Encyclopedia, “Tobias”; Jewish Encyclopedia, “Tobit, Book of”

circle.name: Anna, his wife
circle.text: She kept them by weaving when he went blind, and gave him a sharp answer over the kid. When Tobias left she wept, and every day she watched the road. She saw him coming first.

circle.name: Tobias, his son
circle.text: He made the journey, married Sarah and healed his father's eyes. He buried both his parents, and died at Ecbatana at 127, glad to hear that Nineveh had fallen.

circle.name: Sarah, his daughter-in-law
circle.text: Seven husbands had died before their marriage began. Tobit went out to the gate of Nineveh to meet her, and blessed her: “Welcome, daughter!”

circle.name: Raphael, the angel
circle.text: He went with Tobias as Azarias, a kinsman hired for a drachma a day. He told Tobit that he had been with him each time he buried the dead.

circle.name: Achiacharus, his nephew
circle.text: The king's cupbearer and keeper of the accounts. He brought Tobit home after he fled, cared for him when he went blind, and came to the wedding feast.

circle.name: Deborah, his grandmother
circle.text: His father's mother. Tobit was left an orphan, and she taught him to give a third tenth of his harvest away.

circle.name: Gabael
circle.text: The man in Rages of Media who kept Tobit's ten talents of silver, sealed in their bags, until the angel came for them.

circle.name: Sennacherib, king of Assyria
circle.text: He killed many exiles in his rage, looked for Tobit to put him to death, and took everything he had. Two of his own sons killed him.

death.big: He died in Nineveh, very old, in his bed, with his son and grandsons around him.
paras: He called Tobias and his six sons. He told them to leave Nineveh, for he believed what the prophet Jonah had said against it. Jerusalem would be laid waste and its temple burned, he said. But God would bring His people home, and all the nations would turn to Him.

“Bury me decently, and your mother with me. Don't stay at Nineveh.” While he was still speaking, “he gave up the ghost in the bed.” The Greek text on this page gives his age as 158; Jerome's Latin says 102.
Tobias gave him a great funeral, and later buried Anna beside him. Then he took his family to Ecbatana, to Sarah's parents. Before he died, he heard that Nineveh had fallen.

items.q: My child, take your sons. Behold, I have grown old, and am ready to depart out of this life.
And now, my children, consider what alms does, and how righteousness delivers.

saint.big: No church calendar we checked gives him a day of his own. Catholic and Orthodox Christians read his book as Scripture, and honour the angel of his story.

paras: Rome's book of martyrs, in its 1916 edition, does keep a Tobias on 2 November. He is a different man: a martyr of Sebaste, under the emperor Licinius.

The angel of his story has days of his own. Rome kept St Raphael on 24 October from 1921, and since 1969 he shares 29 September with Michael and Gabriel. The Orthodox keep him on 8 November with the other archangels.

Anglicans still pray Tobit's words. The Church of England's *Common Worship* sets verses of his song as a canticle, “A Song of Tobit”. The Episcopal Church reads from his book on the days of Hugh of Lincoln and Elizabeth of Hungary, 17 and 19 November.
